title: The Peterman Pod × Ethan Evans — 往白的那头说宽一点
title_en: The Peterman Pod × Ethan Evans — Stretch Toward the White End

questions.question: 一位前 Amazon VP 在讲「高管气场」时随口说「带数字的说法可信度高 62%」，随即承认这个数字是他当场编的。这一幕最直接地揭示了「把自己说宽一点」为什么管用？
options: 精确的数字能体现说话人的专业素养，因此数字本身就是可信度的来源
听众更在意说话人的职位和资历，内容真假并不影响他们的判断
人们其实知道这类数字多半是编的，但出于礼貌不会当面点破
听的人通常不去核查，一个具体又说得笃定的说法就足以被当真
questions.explanation: 节目点出这条线的落点：说宽之所以管用，是因为听的人不核查，62% 就是当场的证明。数字只是让说法听起来具体，它本身并不提供可信度，真正起作用的是没人去查；同一期里他引用的气场公式也和原始出处对不上。
questions.question_en: While discussing executive presence, a former Amazon VP tossed out that "claims with numbers are 62% more believable," then admitted he had just made the figure up. What does this moment most directly reveal about why stretching your claims works?
options_en: Precise figures signal the speaker's expertise, so the number itself is what makes a claim credible
Audiences care more about the speaker's title and seniority, so whether the content is true doesn't matter
People actually know such figures are mostly invented but are too polite to say so to the speaker's face
Listeners usually don't check, so a specific claim delivered with confidence is enough to be believed
questions.explanation_en: The episode lands on this point: stretching works because listeners don't verify, and the 62% figure proved it on the spot. The number only makes a claim sound specific; credibility comes from nobody checking. Even the executive-presence formula he cited in the same episode didn't match its original source.

questions.question: 经理手上只有一个好项目，一位下属天天来要，另一位从不吭声。按节目中对经理心理的描述，安静的那位通常会怎样？
options: 经理会告诉自己「以后再补偿他」，然后一直没补上，等待越久越被跳过
经理会按两人的实际能力分配，安静与否对结果影响不大，最终公平
经理会把项目给安静的那位，因为不争不抢在经理眼里代表更可靠
经理会意识到自己在亏待老实人，于是在下一次机会里优先补偿给他
questions.explanation: 经理不会对自己说「我在亏待老实人」，而是合理化成「以后再补偿」，结果永远补不上。这就像操作系统里没有实现「老化」的调度器：按谁吵谁先排，低优先级进程会一直饿着。以为经理会意识到并主动补偿，恰好低估了人作为「合理化机器」的能力。
questions.question_en: A manager has one good project. One report asks for it every day; the other never speaks up. According to the episode's account of how managers think, what usually happens to the quiet one?
options_en: The manager tells themselves "I'll make it up to them later," never does, and the longer they wait the more they're skipped
The manager assigns work on actual ability, so being quiet makes little difference and things end up fair
The manager gives them the project, because not pushing comes across as more reliable in a manager's eyes
The manager realizes they're shortchanging the nice person and makes sure to compensate them at the next opportunity
questions.explanation_en: Managers don't tell themselves "I'm shortchanging the nice people"; they rationalize it as "I'll make it up later" and never do. It's like an OS scheduler without aging: serve whoever is loudest and low-priority processes starve. Expecting the manager to notice and compensate underestimates people as "rationalization machines."

questions.question: 如果每个人都把职场政治的招数玩到最优，节目里给出的判断和建议是什么？
options: 这会让真正有实力的人脱颖而出，因为各种手段被拉平之后，大家比的就只剩下技术能力
这会变成人人互捅、回到原点的囚徒困境，与其玩得更狠，不如换一张对手更弱的牌桌
这会让组织迅速崩溃，所以应该主动退出政治游戏，专心把本职工作做到无可挑剔
这会逼出更高明的玩法，所以要比别人更早学会更暗的招数，才能保住自己的位置
questions.explanation: 他把人人玩到最优的局面比作囚徒困境，结果是互相抵消、原地不动（类似红皇后效应）。他的对策是换桌，找自己几项能力交集里几乎没人竞争的位置，比如在大公司学成 AWS 专家后去高增长公司。「学更暗的招」正是他说的不要做的事。
questions.question_en: If everyone played office politics optimally, what does the episode conclude, and what does it advise?
options_en: It lets the truly skilled rise, because once tactics cancel out, the only thing left to compete on is technical ability
It becomes a prisoner's dilemma where everyone stabs everyone and ends up back at zero, so rather than play harder, move to a table with weaker opponents
It quickly destroys the organization, so you should opt out of politics entirely and make your own work beyond reproach
It forces ever cleverer play, so you need to learn darker tactics before others do just to hold your position
questions.explanation_en: He frames universal optimal play as a prisoner's dilemma: everything cancels out and nobody moves (a Red Queen effect). His answer is to change tables — find the intersection of skills where almost no one competes, like becoming an AWS expert at Amazon and then joining a high-growth company. Learning darker tactics is exactly what he advises against.
